questions.question: An initially alive life has an annuity with predetermined payments 1, 2 and 3 at years 0, 1 and 2 respectively, conditional on survival to each date. Which mortality model is needed for these changing amounts?
options: A separate independent lifetime model for each different payment amount.
One lifetime model, with survival assessed separately at each payment date.
One lifetime model that must reuse first-year survival for all later dates.
Only the death probability at year 2, applied equally to every receipt.

questions.question: An annuity pays 1 now, 2 at year 1 and 3 at year 2 while alive. An analyst discounts each amount from its own date, then multiplies their sum by $P(T>2)$, where $T$ is future lifetime. Assume $P(1<T\le2)>0$. Which error is guaranteed?
options: It counts a payment after death for lives dying before year 2.
It discounts every payment from year 2 instead of its own date.
It discards earlier receipts of lives not reaching the last date.
It counts the certain initial payment twice on every outcome.

questions.question: Two receipts refer to the same future lifetime $T$ and dates $0<s<t$. Which expression gives $P(T>s,\ T>t)$ for every lifetime law?
options: $P(T>s)P(T>t)$
$P(s<T\leq t)$

questions.question: For a finite varying annuity, $Y=\sum_k b_kv^{t_k}\mathbf1_{\{T>t_k\}}$, where $b_k\geq0$ are predetermined amounts, $t_k\geq0$ payment times, $v>0$ a discount factor and $T$ one future lifetime. What role does independence of its receipt indicators play in calculating $E[Y]$?
options: It is required, otherwise even a finite sum has no APV formula.
It is automatic because the payment amounts are predetermined.
It is required only for receipts with different benefit amounts.
It is unnecessary: expectation adds the individually weighted receipts.

questions.question: A life annuity pays continuously at rate 1 per year before time 1 and rate 3 per year after time 1, stopping at death. No lump-sum receipt is specified. For a life surviving beyond time 1, does the jump in rate create a separate payment of 2 at that instant?
options: Yes; the increase of 2 is paid separately at time 1.
No; it changes the later rate without adding a point payment.
No; instead all earlier payments are repriced at rate 3.
Yes; the rate 3 is paid once, replacing all subsequent receipts.

questions.question: A varying annuity pays 1 at issue, 2 at year 1 and 4 at year 2 while the insured is alive. Annual discount factor is 0.9. The realised lifetime is 1.5 years. What is its realised PV?
For an initially alive life, a varying annuity pays 1 now and 2 next year if the life survives. Annual discount factor is 0.95 and next-year survival probability is 0.9. What is APV?
One receipt in a varying annuity pays 4 at time 0.5 years on survival, whose probability is 0.8. Annual discount factor is 0.81. What is this receipt contribution to APV?
Two receipts in one varying annuity have PVs $X=2(0.5)\mathbf1_{\{T>1\}}$ and $W=3(0.5)^2\mathbf1_{\{T>2\}}$ for the same future lifetime $T$. Given $P(T>1)=0.8$ and $P(T>2)=0.6$, what is $E[XW]$?
A varying annuity pays continuously at rate $b(t)=t$ units per year at elapsed time $t$ while alive. Interest is zero. In the realised scenario future lifetime is $T=2.2$ years. What is total PV?

Two varying-annuity amounts $a,b>0$ are paid at the same time $t>0$ on survival, whose probability is $p\in(0,1)$. With annual discount factor $v>0$, their total PV is $Y=(a+b)v^t\mathbf1_{\{T>t\}}$ for lifetime $T$. Which expression gives $E[Y^2]$ for every such choice of amounts and basis?

Two finite varying annuities use the same life $T$, dates $t_k\geq0$ and positive discount factor $v$. Their predetermined amounts satisfy $b_k\geq c_k\geq0$ at every date. Which APV comparison is guaranteed?
options: The b-schedule APV must be strictly larger on every mortality basis.
The c-schedule APV is larger because its benefits are less concentrated.
The APVs can be compared only if the survival indicators are independent.
The b-schedule APV is at least the c-schedule APV.

questions.question: For a finite varying annuity $Y=\sum_k b_kv^{t_k}I_k$, define $I_k=\mathbf1_{\{T>t_k\}}$ for the same life $T$, with $b_k\geq0$, $t_k\geq0$ and $v>0$. An analyst retains only $\sum_k b_k^2v^{2t_k}E[I_k]$ when computing $E[Y^2]$. What is the general effect?
options: It gives a lower bound, because omitted cross terms are nonnegative.
It gives the exact second moment whenever the payment dates differ.
It gives an upper bound because shared survival would double-count receipts.
It gives variance directly because each individual receipt has been squared.

questions.question: A varying annuity pays 2 at year 1 and 4 at year 2 on survival. With future lifetime $T$, annual discount factor is $v=0.8$, $P(T>1)=0.75$ and $P(T>2)=0.5$. If $Y$ is its total PV, what is $E[Y^2]$?
Future lifetime $T$ is uniform on $(0,2)$ years. An annuity pays continuously at rate $b(t)=1$ on $0\leq t<1$ and $b(t)=2$ on $1\leq t<2$, stopping at death. Interest is zero. What is its APV?

A varying annuity pays 2 at year 1 and an unknown amount B at year 2, conditional on survival to each date. Annual discount factor is 0.9, one-year survival is 0.8 and two-year survival is 0.6. Its APV is 3.384. What is B?

An initially alive life has $P(T>k)=2^{-k}$ for every integer $k\geq0$. A varying annuity pays $b_k=(3/2)^k$ at time $k$ while alive, with zero interest. Let $Y$ be total PV. Which assessment correctly checks the finite-second-moment premise?
options: APV and second moment are both infinite because amounts increase without discounting.
APV is 4, but the second moment is infinite.
APV is 4 and second moment is 16 because expectation can be squared.
APV and second moment are both finite because death occurs at a finite time.

questions.question: For one life at dates $0<s<t$, define indicators $I_s=\mathbf1_{\{T>s\}}$ and $I_t=\mathbf1_{\{T>t\}}$. Their survival probabilities are $a=P(T>s)$ and $b=P(T>t)$, with $0\leq b\leq a\leq1$. What is the necessary and sufficient condition for these two indicators to be independent?
options: $a=b$

questions.question: A varying annuity pays one unit at each of years 1 and 2 on survival, with zero interest. Write $Y=\mathbf1_{\{T>1\}}+\mathbf1_{\{T>2\}}$ for one continuous future lifetime $T>0$. Its APV is fixed at $E[Y]=1$, but its mortality basis may vary. What is the complete feasible range of $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$?

A life has one-year survival 0.99 and two-year survival 0.5. Annual discount factor is 0.9. Compare a unit receipt at year 1 with the same amount instead scheduled at year 2, each conditional on survival to its own date. Which mean-and-variance comparison is correct?
options: The later receipt has both smaller APV and smaller PV variance.
The later receipt has larger APV but smaller PV variance.
The later receipt has smaller APV but larger PV variance.
The later receipt has smaller APV and exactly the same PV variance.
